course.title: Legal
course.desc: Contract review, case summaries, compliance checks, legal research.

exercises.title: Vague vs. precise
exercises.sc:
A partner hands you a 40-page non-disclosure agreement between your client (a biotech company) and a prospective research collaborator. You type:

"Review this NDA."

The AI returns a generic summary that misses the carve-outs for pre-existing IP, the unusual definition of confidential information, and the non-solicitation clause buried in Section 12.
exercises.task: Write a better prompt. Be specific about which NDA provisions matter most, what format you want the analysis in, and what red flags to highlight. Assume your client is the disclosing party sharing proprietary research data.
exercises.hint: A 200-word specification produces better results than a 20-word instruction followed by 15 rounds of correction. Specify: which party you represent, what clauses matter, and what 'red flag' means.
exercises.cr: 1) Specifies which NDA provisions to focus on (e.g., definition of confidential info, exclusions, term, remedies) 2) Defines output format (table, summary, checklist) 3) Identifies what to flag as risky or unusual 4) Clarifies which party the reviewer represents 5) Is substantially more detailed than 'review this NDA'

exercises.title: Specify the output
exercises.sc: A senior associate asks you to "research the current state of non-compete enforceability." You have case law from 6 states, recent FTC rulemaking updates, and several circuit court opinions on the topic.
exercises.task: Write a prompt that specifies exactly what the output should look like. Define the structure — jurisdiction-by-jurisdiction table? Bullet-point summaries? What columns, what comparisons, what level of citation detail?
exercises.hint: If you handed the output to the senior associate, would they immediately have what they need for the client memo without follow-up questions?
exercises.cr: 1) Specifies output format explicitly (table, matrix, or structured summary) 2) Names specific jurisdictions or comparison dimensions 3) Requests citation format or level of detail 4) Defines what 'good' looks like for the intended use

exercises.title: Audience and tone
exercises.sc:
Your firm just completed a trademark opposition proceeding. The client won, but the opposing party may appeal. You need to communicate the outcome to:

1. The client's general counsel (strategic, next-steps focused)
2. The court via a proposed order (formal, procedural)
3. The client's marketing team (plain language, practical implications)
exercises.task: Write a prompt for ONE audience that explicitly controls tone, length, legal terminology level, and emphasis. Make it clear who the reader is and what they need from this communication.
exercises.hint: General counsel wants the legal implications in two paragraphs. The marketing team wants to know 'can we keep using the logo?'
exercises.cr: 1) Clearly identifies target audience 2) Specifies tone and formality level 3) Defines what to emphasize vs. omit 4) Sets appropriate use of legal jargon 5) Shows audience-aware framing of the same facts

exercises.title: Setting constraints
exercises.sc: You're asking the AI to draft a motion for summary judgment. Without constraints, the AI either produces a 300-word stub that reads like a blog post or a 5,000-word treatise filled with speculative arguments and non-existent case citations.
exercises.task: Write a prompt with explicit constraints: page limit, required sections, citation rules, what arguments NOT to include, formatting per local court rules, and tone requirements.
exercises.hint: Telling the AI what to avoid is just as valuable as telling it what to do. 'Do not fabricate case citations' is a critical constraint for legal AI work.
exercises.cr: 1) Sets specific length or page constraint 2) Includes 'do not' instructions (e.g., no fabricated citations) 3) Lists required sections (introduction, statement of facts, argument, conclusion) 4) Specifies formatting rules 5) Demonstrates negative constraints relevant to legal drafting

exercises.title: Role assignment
exercises.sc: You've drafted a licensing agreement for your client, the licensor. Before sending it to opposing counsel, you want the AI to review it — but generic feedback won't help. The review depends entirely on whose perspective the AI takes.
exercises.task: Write a prompt that assigns the AI a specific role — for example, "You are experienced opposing counsel representing the licensee, reviewing this agreement to identify terms that are unfavorable to your client." Define what expertise and adversarial perspective to apply.
exercises.hint: A 'licensee's outside counsel' catches different issues than a 'regulatory compliance officer' or a 'commercial litigator evaluating enforceability.'
exercises.cr: 1) Assigns a specific legal role with credentials 2) Defines what expertise or adversarial perspective to apply 3) Specifies what to evaluate or flag 4) Role choice meaningfully shapes the nature of feedback

exercises.title: Iterative refinement
exercises.sc:
You asked the AI to draft an indemnification clause for a SaaS vendor agreement and got:

"The Vendor shall indemnify the Client against all claims arising from the Vendor's services. The Client shall notify the Vendor of any claims promptly."

It's missing carve-outs, a liability cap, control-of-defense provisions, and the mutual indemnification your client needs.
exercises.task: Write a follow-up prompt that fixes this. Don't start over — refine. Tell the AI specifically what's wrong and what to add or change in the clause.
exercises.hint: Good refinement is surgical: 'Add a carve-out for claims arising from Client's modification of the deliverables, include a control-of-defense provision, and cap indemnification at 2x annual fees.' Bad: 'Make it more thorough.'
exercises.cr: 1) References specific problems in the draft clause 2) Gives targeted corrections with legal specifics 3) Adds missing provisions (carve-outs, caps, procedures) 4) Shows refinement over restarting 5) Demonstrates iterative improvement cycle

exercises.title: Plan before you ask
exercises.sc:
A partner asks you to prepare a comprehensive legal research memorandum on whether your client's employee non-solicitation agreements are enforceable under recent changes in state law. If you just say "write a legal memo on non-solicits," you'll get a law school outline, not a practitioner memo.

The principle: spend 10 minutes planning to save an hour of corrections.
exercises.task: Write a detailed specification prompt (150-250 words). Include: the legal question presented, jurisdiction, governing standards, required sections, depth of analysis, citation expectations, audience (partner, client, or court), and what to exclude.
exercises.hint: Your specification IS the prompt. The more precise the spec, the better the first draft. Include the standard of review, burden of proof, and which side you represent.
exercises.cr: 1) Defines the legal question precisely 2) Specifies jurisdiction and governing law 3) Lists required memo sections (question presented, brief answer, discussion, conclusion) 4) Sets citation expectations 5) Includes exclusions and scope limits 6) Spec itself is 100+ words

exercises.title: Chain-of-thought
exercises.sc: Your client is a software company sued for patent infringement. You have the patent claims, the accused product specification, and a prior art reference. The partner wants a preliminary infringement analysis before the Markman hearing.
exercises.task: Write a prompt forcing step-by-step legal analysis: first parse each patent claim element, then map elements to the accused product features, then identify gaps or non-literal equivalents, then assess overall infringement likelihood. Use explicit step numbering.
exercises.hint: Chain-of-thought: 'Before giving your conclusion, first do X, then Y, then Z.' Patent claim construction requires methodical element-by-element analysis — perfect for step-by-step prompting.
exercises.cr: 1) Uses explicit numbered steps 2) Separates claim parsing from infringement mapping 3) Asks for reasoning before conclusions 4) Includes a scoring or likelihood assessment 5) Steps build logically from claim construction to infringement opinion

exercises.title: Few-shot examples
exercises.sc:
You're building a system to categorize contract clauses across hundreds of vendor agreements for a due diligence review. Categories: Indemnification, Limitation of Liability, Termination, IP Ownership, Confidentiality, Payment Terms, Governing Law, Force Majeure.

Examples:
• "Vendor shall defend and hold harmless Client from third-party IP claims" → Indemnification
• "This Agreement shall be governed by the laws of the State of New York" → Governing Law
• "Either party may terminate upon 60 days written notice" → Termination
exercises.task: Write a prompt using few-shot examples that teaches the AI to categorize new contract clauses. Include examples in consistent format, define all categories, add 2-3 test clauses to classify.
exercises.hint: Format consistency matters: if examples use '→', use '→' for all of them. Include at least one ambiguous clause that could belong to multiple categories.
exercises.cr: 1) Includes 3+ clear example clause-category pairs 2) Defines all categories 3) Examples cover multiple categories 4) Includes new test clauses for classification 5) Consistent format throughout

exercises.title: Structured output
exercises.sc: You've been asked to prepare a regulatory compliance checklist for a fintech client launching a consumer lending product in three states. Instead of a narrative memo, the compliance team wants a structured risk matrix they can track in a spreadsheet.
exercises.task: Write a prompt that enforces specific output structure. Define exact columns (regulation, jurisdiction, requirement, compliance status, risk level, remediation steps), what goes in each, risk level criteria, and how to handle overlapping or conflicting requirements.
exercises.hint: Show the exact format you want. Include an example row so the AI understands precisely what level of detail is expected.
exercises.cr: 1) Defines exact table structure with named columns 2) Explains what goes in each column 3) Provides risk level criteria (e.g., High/Medium/Low with definitions) 4) Handles edge cases like conflicting multi-state requirements 5) Optionally includes example row

exercises.title: Compare and evaluate
exercises.sc:
Two associates drafted competing arguments for a motion to compel discovery. Both address the same relevance and proportionality issues under FRCP Rule 26(b)(1), but take different approaches:

Argument A focuses on the broad scope of permissible discovery and cites liberal interpretation case law.

Argument B takes a targeted approach, linking each document request to a specific claim element and demonstrating proportionality.
exercises.task: Write a prompt that evaluates both arguments against specific legal effectiveness criteria and recommends which to use. Define 3-4 criteria, ask for per-criterion scores, and require a justified recommendation.
exercises.hint: Don't ask 'which is better?' Instead: 'Score each 1-5 on legal authority strength, persuasiveness to this judge's known preferences, proportionality analysis, and strategic risk.'
exercises.cr: 1) Defines 3+ evaluation criteria relevant to legal brief quality 2) Asks for per-criterion scores 3) Requires reasoning for each score 4) Requests justified recommendation 5) Criteria are meaningful and non-overlapping

exercises.title: Multi-step decomposition
exercises.sc:
Partner assigns: "Prepare our client for the upcoming breach-of-contract trial. I need witness prep materials, a trial brief outline, exhibit analysis, and jury instruction recommendations."

Too big for one prompt. Needs decomposition into a workflow.
exercises.task: Write a SEQUENCE of 3-4 prompts that decompose this case preparation task. Each prompt builds on the previous output. Show the full chain from fact gathering through trial-ready deliverables.
exercises.hint: Workflow: Fact extraction → Legal issue mapping → Document/witness analysis → Trial strategy synthesis. Each step has clear input and output.
exercises.cr: 1) Breaks into 3+ sequential prompts 2) Each has a focused legal objective 3) Later prompts reference earlier outputs 4) Covers facts → analysis → strategy → deliverables 5) Demonstrates practical case preparation decomposition

exercises.title: Error correction
exercises.sc:
The AI produced this analysis of a contract dispute:

"The defendant breached Section 4.2 by failing to deliver on time. Under the UCC, buyer is entitled to cover damages. Recommendation: file for specific performance immediately."

Problems: assumes UCC applies without checking if it's a services contract, conflates cover damages with specific performance (contradictory remedies), and ignores the force majeure clause the defendant will invoke.
exercises.task: Write a prompt correcting these legal errors. Ask for proper analysis of the governing law question, correct remedy analysis, and consideration of available defenses.
exercises.hint: Point out exactly what's wrong: 'You assumed UCC governs without analyzing whether this is a goods or services contract. Also, cover damages and specific performance are alternative remedies — you can't recommend both.'
exercises.cr: 1) Identifies specific legal errors 2) Asks for correct governing law analysis (UCC vs. common law) 3) Addresses the remedies contradiction 4) Requires consideration of defenses 5) Shows critical legal reasoning

exercises.title: Persona prompting
exercises.sc:
Your firm is preparing for a moot court exercise on a wrongful termination case. You want the AI to stress-test arguments from three perspectives:

1. The trial judge (procedural sufficiency, evidentiary issues)
2. Plaintiff's counsel (employee rights, damages theory)
3. Defense counsel (at-will doctrine, legitimate business reasons)
exercises.task: Write a prompt that has the AI adopt each persona sequentially, critique the case from that perspective, then synthesize the three viewpoints into a unified case strategy assessment.
exercises.hint: Each persona surfaces different concerns. The judge focuses on motions practice. Plaintiff's counsel pushes pretext arguments. Defense counsel looks for burden-of-proof gaps.
exercises.cr: 1) Defines 3 distinct legal personas 2) Each has specific legal concerns and analytical focus 3) Sequential analysis from each perspective 4) Requests synthesis into unified assessment 5) Shows how persona shapes legal analysis

exercises.title: Prompt templates
exercises.sc: You review contracts weekly for new vendor onboarding: identify risky clauses, compare to your firm's standard terms, flag deviations, and produce a recommendation memo. Instead of writing a new prompt each time, you want a reusable template.
exercises.task: Create a reusable prompt template with [BRACKET] variables. Include: contract type, party names, your client's position, standard terms reference, risk tolerance, output format, and recipient. Should work for any contract review.
exercises.hint: Variables like [CONTRACT_TYPE], [CLIENT_NAME], [COUNTERPARTY], [RISK_TOLERANCE], [RECIPIENT] make it reusable — swap in values for each new engagement.
exercises.cr: 1) Uses clear bracket variables 2) Genuinely reusable for any contract review 3) Covers input/analysis/output/recipient 4) 4+ variable placeholders 5) Would save time on recurring contract reviews

exercises.title: Contract due diligence
exercises.sc: Your firm is representing the buyer in a $50M acquisition of a healthcare IT company. You've been assigned 200+ contracts from the virtual data room. The partner needs a due diligence summary by Friday: key risk areas, change-of-control provisions, assignability issues, and any contracts that could blow up the deal.
exercises.task: Write a prompt that produces a structured due diligence analysis: contract categories, risk levels with defined criteria, a tracking table with clause references, deal-breaker flags, and a priority action list.
exercises.hint: Structure your prompt like a professional due diligence checklist: what to extract from each contract, how to assess risk, and how to present findings to the deal team.
exercises.cr: 1) Lists contract categories to review (customer, vendor, employment, IP, lease) 2) Defines risk criteria for due diligence context 3) Specifies table output with clause references 4) Includes deal-breaker flagging mechanism 5) Covers change-of-control and assignability 6) Professional output suitable for partner review

exercises.title: Case docket management
exercises.sc: You return from a two-week trial to find 45 pending matters on your docket. Deadlines range from tomorrow to three months out. Some have court-imposed deadlines, others are client-set. You need to triage immediately: what's at risk of malpractice, what needs attention this week, and what can wait.
exercises.task: Write a prompt that categorizes docket items by urgency and required action. Define categories, deadline types (court-ordered vs. contractual vs. internal), and a scannable output format that a paralegal can act on.
exercises.hint: Priority Matrix: Court deadlines (non-negotiable) > Statute of limitations > Client contractual deadlines > Internal deadlines. Missing a court deadline is malpractice; missing an internal deadline is embarrassing.
exercises.cr: 1) Defines triage categories with legal-specific urgency levels 2) Distinguishes deadline types (court-ordered, statutory, contractual, internal) 3) Flags malpractice-risk items 4) Scannable output format 5) Practical for real docket management

exercises.title: Deposition summary
exercises.sc: You just took a 4-hour deposition of the plaintiff in a products liability case. The court reporter will take two weeks for the transcript, but the partner wants a summary now from your rough notes. Topics covered: product use history, injury timeline, prior medical conditions, expert consultation, and damages claimed.
exercises.task: Write a prompt transforming rough deposition notes into structured deposition summaries: sections by topic, key admissions with page/line references, impeachment material, follow-up items, and handling of ambiguous or evasive answers.
exercises.hint: Template: Witness info, Key Admissions, Contradictions/Impeachment Material, Damages Testimony, Open Issues for Follow-Up.
exercises.cr: 1) Defines output sections appropriate for deposition summaries 2) Key admissions flagged with references 3) Identifies impeachment material and contradictions 4) Prioritizes legally significant testimony over background 5) Includes follow-up action items

exercises.title: Settlement comparison
exercises.sc:
Your client has received three settlement offers in an employment discrimination case:
• Offer A: $275K lump sum, confidentiality clause, no admission of liability, mutual non-disparagement
• Offer B: $180K + reinstatement to former position, no confidentiality, employer issues corrective action memo
• Offer C: $350K structured over 3 years, confidentiality, non-compete for 18 months, full release of all claims

Client needs a clear comparison to make an informed decision.
exercises.task: Write a prompt for a structured settlement comparison: monetary analysis (present value, tax implications), non-monetary terms, risk assessment of each option, client-priority weighting, and a recommendation framework.
exercises.hint: Include: net present value calculation, tax treatment differences (wage vs. emotional distress damages), enforceability of non-compete, and client's stated priorities (money vs. vindication vs. career impact).
exercises.cr: 1) All relevant comparison dimensions (monetary, non-monetary, risk) 2) Clear timeframe and present-value analysis 3) Explicit assumptions about tax treatment and discount rates 4) Summary comparison table 5) Recommendation framework tied to client priorities 6) Addresses enforceability of restrictive terms

exercises.title: Legal memorandum
exercises.sc: The managing partner wants a 10-page legal memorandum on your firm's exposure to a potential class action over a data breach affecting 50,000 client records. The memo goes to the firm's executive committee and outside insurance counsel. It must be thorough, cite authority, and include a recommended course of action.
exercises.task: Write the specification prompt — the detailed brief for a litigation-ready memorandum on the first try. Structure, length per section, citation requirements, legal standards, tone, and exclusions.
exercises.hint: This is the ultimate 'plan before you ask' exercise. A 200-word spec saves hours of revision. Specify: applicable statutes, standard of care, damages theories, and the audience's decision-making needs.
exercises.cr: 1) Defines full memo structure with section headings 2) Length guidance per section 3) Citation and legal authority requirements 4) Specifies applicable legal standards and statutes 5) Exclusions clearly stated 6) Spec is 150+ words 7) Would produce memo suitable for executive committee review

exercises.title: Settlement negotiation comms
exercises.sc:
After 18 months of litigation, you need to communicate a difficult settlement recommendation to your client. The case was strong initially, but a key witness recanted and the judge excluded your expert's damages testimony. The best realistic outcome at trial is now worse than the current $400K settlement offer. Your client originally expected $1.2M.

You need:
1. A letter to the client explaining the recommendation to settle
2. A response to opposing counsel accepting the offer with conditions
3. Internal memo to the file documenting the advice given
exercises.task: Write one prompt producing all three documents with different tones but consistent facts. Address the sensitive nature of delivering unwelcome news to the client while maintaining professional obligations.
exercises.hint: Facts identical across documents, framing changes. The client letter must be empathetic but honest. The letter to opposing counsel must be strategic. The file memo must be thorough for malpractice protection.
exercises.cr: 1) Requests all three documents 2) Different tones for each audience 3) Consistent facts across all three 4) Addresses client expectations management 5) Handles the difficult conversation authentically 6) Demonstrates strategic legal communication

exercises.title: Expert witness vetting
exercises.sc: You're preparing for a medical malpractice trial and need to retain an expert witness on emergency room standard of care. You have CVs from four candidates. The expert must survive a Daubert challenge, have credible testimony experience, and not have conflicts with the defendant hospital system.
exercises.task: Write a prompt creating a systematic expert vetting framework: scored criteria with weights (qualifications, testimony history, Daubert track record, conflicts, fee reasonableness), must-have vs. nice-to-have, red flags, and a ranked recommendation.
exercises.hint: Chain-of-thought: extract qualifications → check Daubert history → assess conflicts → score against criteria → rank → recommend. An expert excluded under Daubert can lose the case.
exercises.cr: 1) Scored criteria with weights 2) Must-haves vs. nice-to-haves (e.g., board certification, prior testimony) 3) Red flags (excluded under Daubert, professional sanctions, conflicts) 4) Comparison table 5) Reasoning behind rankings 6) Multiple techniques combined

exercises.title: Case portfolio review
exercises.sc:
End of quarter. You manage a portfolio of 30 active litigation matters across practice areas: 8 commercial disputes, 6 employment cases, 5 IP matters, 4 regulatory investigations, 4 insurance coverage disputes, and 3 personal injury cases. The managing partner wants:
1. Risk categorization of every matter
2. Settlement vs. trial recommendations
3. Resource allocation priorities
4. Budget variance analysis
5. A 2-page executive summary for the management committee
exercises.task: Write a comprehensive prompt for this end-to-end portfolio review. Use few-shot for matter categorization, chain-of-thought for risk assessment, structured output for the tracking matrix, and templates for the executive summary.
exercises.hint: Capstone: combine every technique. Few-shot + structured output + chain-of-thought + planning + persona prompting. This is how senior litigators actually manage portfolios.
exercises.cr: 1) Few-shot examples for matter categorization 2) Clear risk categories with defined criteria 3) Chain-of-thought for settlement vs. trial analysis 4) Structured portfolio tracking matrix 5) Executive summary format 6) 3+ techniques combined 7) Reusable quarterly workflow

materials.1:
NON-DISCLOSURE AGREEMENT (Excerpt)
Between: Helios BioSciences, Inc. ("Disclosing Party") and Meridian Research Partners, LLC ("Receiving Party")

Section 1.1 - Definition of Confidential Information
"Confidential Information" means all information, whether written, oral, electronic, or visual, disclosed by Disclosing Party relating to proprietary research data, compound formulations, clinical trial protocols, patient data (de-identified), and business strategies. Includes information disclosed 12 months prior to execution.

Section 2.3 - Exclusions
Confidential Information does not include: (a) information publicly available without breach; (b) information known to Receiving Party prior to disclosure (with written proof); (c) information independently developed without reference to Confidential Information.

Section 4.1 - Non-Solicitation
For 24 months following termination, Receiving Party shall not solicit, hire, or engage any employee, contractor, or consultant of Disclosing Party who had access to Confidential Information.

Section 6.2 - Term and Survival
Agreement effective for 3 years. Confidentiality obligations survive for 7 years after expiration. Non-solicitation survives for 24 months after termination.

Section 8.1 - Remedies
Disclosing Party entitled to injunctive relief without posting bond. Receiving Party shall pay all reasonable attorney fees incurred in enforcement.

Section 9.4 - Return of Materials
Within 10 business days of termination, Receiving Party shall return or certify destruction of all Confidential Information. No copies retained except as required by law.
materials.2:
CASE LAW RESEARCH — NON-COMPETE ENFORCEABILITY

California: Business & Professions Code § 16600 — Non-competes void except in sale-of-business context. Edwards v. Arthur Andersen (2008) — Supreme Court confirmed near-total ban.

Texas: Tex. Bus. & Com. Code § 15.50 — Enforceable if ancillary to an otherwise enforceable agreement, reasonable in scope/geography/duration. Marsh USA v. Cook (2011) — stock options can constitute consideration.

New York: No statute. Common law test: reasonable in duration/geography/scope, necessary to protect legitimate interest, not unduly burdensome. BDO Seidman v. Hirshberg (1999) — partial enforcement (blue pencil).

Illinois: 770 ILCS 90/1 (Freedom to Work Act, 2022) — Cannot enforce against employees earning under $75K (rising to $90K by 2037). Requires 14-day notice period. Fifield v. Premier Dealer Services (2013) — 2 years employment = adequate consideration.

Massachusetts: M.G.L. c. 149 § 24L (2018) — Max 12 months, garden leave or mutually-agreed consideration required, cannot apply to hourly/non-exempt employees.

Florida: Fla. Stat. § 542.335 — Presumptively reasonable: 6 months (non-solicitation), 2 years (non-compete). Burden on party seeking enforcement shifted to party opposing.
materials.3:
TRADEMARK OPPOSITION OUTCOME — COMMUNICATION MATERIALS

Case: Helios BioSciences, Inc. v. HelioTech Solutions, LLC
TTAB Proceeding No. 91/278,432
Outcome: Opposition sustained; HelioTech application for "HELIOTECH" mark (Class 5, pharmaceutical preparations) refused registration.

Key findings:
- Likelihood of confusion established under DuPont factors
- Marks are similar in sight and sound
- Goods overlap in pharmaceutical/biotech channels
- Helios mark has acquired distinctiveness through 8 years of use

Potential appeal:
- HelioTech has 63 days to appeal to Federal Circuit or file civil action in district court
- Appeal likelihood estimated at 40% based on counsel's assessment

Implications:
- Helios can continue exclusive use of mark in Class 5
- HelioTech may rebrand or narrow to different class
- Marketing team can proceed with planned product launch using existing branding
- Monitor for any new applications by HelioTech in related classes
materials.4:
MOTION FOR SUMMARY JUDGMENT — CONTEXT

Case: DataVault Corp. v. Sterling Industries, Inc.
Court: U.S. District Court, Southern District of New York
Case No. 1:23-cv-04821
Judge: Hon. Patricia Kwan

Claim: Breach of Master Service Agreement (MSA), specifically Section 5.3 (delivery milestones) and Section 8.1 (performance warranties)

Undisputed Facts:
- MSA executed March 15, 2022, for custom ERP implementation
- Total contract value: $2.4M, paid in 6 milestone installments
- Milestones 1-3 delivered on time (March-September 2022)
- Milestone 4 delivered 47 days late (February 2023 vs. December 2022)
- Client rejected Milestone 4 deliverables citing 23 critical defects
- Sterling invokes Section 14.2 (Force Majeure) citing supply chain disruption

Local Rules: S.D.N.Y. Local Civil Rule 56.1 requires statement of undisputed material facts
Page limit: 25 pages per Local Rule 6.1

Standard: Celotex Corp. v. Catrett, 477 U.S. 317 (1986)
materials.5:
LICENSING AGREEMENT DRAFT (Key Terms)

Licensor: NovaTech Solutions, Inc.
Licensee: Pacific Rim Enterprises, Ltd.
Subject: Exclusive license to NovaTech's proprietary supply chain optimization software ("Licensed Technology")

Section 2.1 - Grant of License
Exclusive, non-transferable license to use Licensed Technology in Asia-Pacific region for 5-year term.

Section 3.2 - Royalty
8% of net revenue derived from use of Licensed Technology, payable quarterly. Minimum annual royalty: $500,000 regardless of revenue.

Section 4.1 - IP Ownership
All IP rights in Licensed Technology remain with Licensor. Improvements developed by Licensee using Licensed Technology are jointly owned.

Section 5.3 - Audit Rights
Licensor may audit Licensee's books and records once per calendar year with 30 days notice. Licensee bears audit cost if underpayment exceeds 5%.

Section 7.2 - Termination
Licensor may terminate for: (a) material breach uncured for 30 days; (b) bankruptcy filing; (c) failure to meet minimum royalty for 2 consecutive quarters.

Section 9.1 - Non-Compete
During term and 2 years post-termination, Licensee shall not develop, license, or distribute competing technology in the licensed territory.
materials.6:
ORIGINAL INDEMNIFICATION CLAUSE

"The Vendor shall indemnify the Client against all claims arising from the Vendor's services. The Client shall notify the Vendor of any claims promptly."

ACTUAL CONTRACT REQUIREMENTS:
- SaaS platform agreement, $400K annual value
- Both parties need mutual indemnification
- Client's concerns: IP infringement claims, data breaches, regulatory violations
- Vendor's concerns: Client misuse, unauthorized modifications, third-party integrations
- Liability cap needed: discussion around 2x annual fees
- Insurance requirement: $5M commercial general liability, $2M cyber liability
- Control of defense: indemnifying party controls, but indemnified party can participate
- Notice period: 15 business days of becoming aware of claim
- Carve-outs needed for: willful misconduct, breach of confidentiality, IP infringement (uncapped)
materials.7:
LEGAL RESEARCH MEMO — CONTEXT

Client: Cascade Digital Marketing, Inc. (250 employees, headquartered in Illinois)
Question: Are our employee non-solicitation agreements enforceable under the Illinois Freedom to Work Act (effective Jan 1, 2022)?

Relevant facts:
- Non-solicits signed by all employees earning above $50K
- Agreements restrict soliciting clients AND co-workers for 18 months post-employment
- No additional consideration provided beyond continued employment
- Three recent departures took clients with them
- One departing employee earning $68K (below $90K threshold for non-solicits)

Jurisdiction: Illinois (primary), with employees in Indiana and Wisconsin
Governing statute: 770 ILCS 90/1 et seq.
Key issues:
- Income threshold for non-solicitation ($45K in 2022, escalating)
- Adequacy of consideration (continued employment vs. new consideration)
- Reasonableness of 18-month duration
- Interaction with other states' laws for remote employees

Memo audience: Litigation partner evaluating enforcement action
materials.8:
PATENT INFRINGEMENT ANALYSIS — MATERIALS

U.S. Patent No. 10,456,789 — "System and Method for Real-Time Inventory Prediction Using Machine Learning"
Patent Holder: Apex Analytics, Inc.
Accused Infringer: Our client, ShelfSmart Technologies, Inc.

Claim 1 (Independent):
"A system comprising:
(a) a data ingestion module configured to receive point-of-sale transaction data in real-time;
(b) a machine learning engine trained on historical sales patterns to generate predictive demand models;
(c) a threshold comparison module that compares predicted demand against current inventory levels;
(d) an alert generation module that transmits restocking notifications to designated supply chain endpoints when predicted demand exceeds a configurable threshold."

Accused Product: ShelfSmart "DemandPulse" Platform
- Receives POS data via API integration (batch processing every 15 minutes, not real-time streaming)
- Uses statistical regression models (not ML in traditional sense — no neural networks or training datasets)
- Compares forecasted demand to inventory via dashboard (manual review, not automated comparison)
- Sends email alerts to store managers when inventory falls below static reorder point (not configurable per-SKU threshold)

Prior Art Reference:
U.S. Patent No. 8,234,567 (filed 2009) — "Automated Inventory Replenishment System" — discloses elements (a) and (c) but uses rule-based logic, not ML.
materials.9:
CONTRACT CLAUSES TO CATEGORIZE

1. "In no event shall either party's aggregate liability exceed the total fees paid in the preceding 12-month period."

2. "Vendor shall maintain all source code in escrow with Iron Mountain. Upon Vendor's insolvency, Client receives immediate access."

3. "All disputes arising under this Agreement shall be resolved through binding arbitration in Chicago, IL under AAA Commercial Rules."

4. "Client grants Vendor a limited, non-exclusive license to use Client's trademarks solely for purposes of performing the Services."

5. "Either party may terminate this Agreement immediately upon written notice if the other party makes an assignment for the benefit of creditors."

6. "Vendor shall not increase fees by more than 3% annually, with 60 days prior written notice."

FINTECH COMPLIANCE CONTEXT

Client: BrightLend, Inc. — launching consumer lending product (personal loans $1K-$50K)
Launch jurisdictions: California, New York, Texas

Key Regulatory Framework:
- Federal: Truth in Lending Act (TILA/Reg Z), Equal Credit Opportunity Act (ECOA/Reg B), Fair Debt Collection Practices Act (FDCPA), CFPB Supervision
- California: California Financing Law (CFL), Cal. Fin. Code § 22000+, CA Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA)
- New York: NY Banking Law Article 9 (Licensed Lender), NY DFS regulations, interest rate caps (civil usury 16%, criminal usury 25%)
- Texas: TX Finance Code Ch. 342 (Consumer Loans), no general usury cap for licensed lenders but rate must be disclosed

Overlapping requirements:
- All three states require lending licenses (different applications)
- TILA disclosure requirements overlap with state-specific disclosure rules
- NY and CA have stricter privacy requirements than federal baseline
- TX has fewer restrictions but unique bonding requirements

Conflicts:
- NY caps interest at 25% criminally; TX has no equivalent cap for licensed lenders
- CA requires specific adverse action notice language that differs from federal ECOA template
- Fee structures permitted in TX may violate NY or CA rules
materials.11:
MOTION TO COMPEL — COMPETING ARGUMENTS

Case: Pinnacle Health Systems v. Dr. James Kershaw et al.
Dispute: Non-compete enforcement; defendant physicians left plaintiff hospital system and opened competing practice within restricted area.

Document Requests at Issue: Plaintiff seeks all patient communications, scheduling data, and financial records from defendants' new practice for the 6-month period since opening.

ARGUMENT A (Broad Discovery Approach):
"Under FRCP 26(b)(1), parties may obtain discovery regarding any nonprivileged matter relevant to any party's claim or defense and proportional to the needs of the case. The requested documents are directly relevant to establishing the extent of patient diversion and quantifying damages. Courts routinely permit broad discovery in non-compete cases. See Coca-Cola Bottling Co. v. Coca-Cola Co., 107 F.R.D. 288 (D. Del. 1985) (liberal construction of relevance in commercial disputes)."

ARGUMENT B (Targeted Discovery Approach):
"Each document request maps to a specific element of Plaintiff's breach-of-covenant claim: (1) patient scheduling data establishes breach of geographic restriction — Claim Element 2; (2) patient origin data proves solicitation of Plaintiff's patients — Claim Element 3; (3) revenue data limited to diverted patients quantifies actual damages — Claim Element 5. This targeted approach satisfies proportionality under FRCP 26(b)(1) while protecting Defendants' patients' privacy interests and avoiding undue burden on a 6-physician practice. See Cates v. Sears, Roebuck & Co., 928 F.2d 679 (5th Cir. 1991) (proportionality requires nexus between discovery and claims)."
